notes:
I've put together notes for Luke 19:1–24, but three things are missing. I found nothing from netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org, nothing from the Catholic sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com), and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings, so those categories are left out. For verse 11 I found nothing on what the parable meant to its first hearers or how it was written; the only historical background below is the Archelaus story.

On "Protestant traditions differ": the sources don't line up neatly by denomination. The real disagreements are over particular questions: verse 8, verse 17, and verses 20–24 (whether the third servant is saved). Where I name a teacher's tradition, that label is my own and doesn't come from the pages.

## Luke 19:1–10 – Zacchaeus

**v. 1**
- Guzik says Jericho was an important ancient city, and Jesus seems to have passed through mainly to meet Zacchaeus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-19/

**v. 2**
- **His job.** Ellicott thinks Zacchaeus was probably a middle-man between the big Roman tax firms and the local collectors who actually took the money. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-2.htm
- **"Chief tax collector."** Guzik quotes Morris: the title appears nowhere else, but it seems to mean the head of the local tax office. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-19/
- **His name.** Guzik notes that "Zacchaeus" means "pure one," which he says the man was not until he received Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-19/
- **"Very wealthy."** Poole says this detail shows God's grace. It proves that a rich man's salvation, while hard, is possible with God (compare Luke 18). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-2.htm
- Henry Morris (in Precept Austin) makes the same link: Luke 19:1–10 is living proof that a rich man can be saved. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-19-commentary

**v. 3**
- **Why he wanted to see Jesus.** Gill says it was at first curiosity, more like Herod's wish to see Jesus than that of the prophets. Barnes adds that this mere curiosity seems to have led to his conversion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-3.htm
- **Calvin's view.** Faith was not yet fully formed, but his eagerness was a preparation for it and showed "some seed of piety." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-1.html
- **Who was short?** Gill notes that some old translations (Syriac, Persian) name Zacchaeus in the clause, so no one would think it was Jesus who was short. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-3.htm
- **Shut out by his job.** Coffman says the crowd wasn't the only barrier: the Pharisees had flatly excluded all tax collectors from God's people. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/luke-19.html#28-40

**v. 4**
- **Climbing the tree.** Guzik says Zacchaeus did something thought beneath a rich grown man. Without knowing it, he became like a child (Matthew 18:3). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-19/
- One old note on Biblehub says his desire beat his sense of honour and shame. It also suggests his house lay further along the road, which would explain why he ran ahead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-3.htm
- **Orthodox reading.** Because Zacchaeus was short, believers who are "short" in spiritual stature must climb the ladder of the virtues. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/2025/02/02/1-sunday-of-zacchaeus

**v. 5**
- **Called by name.** Guzik connects this with John 10:3, where Jesus calls his sheep by name. "Hurry" means the chance could be lost; "come down" means humbling himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-19/
- **Choosing a sinner's house.** The Pulpit Commentary notes Jericho was a city of priests, yet Jesus passed over their houses for a tax collector's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/19.htm

**v. 6**
- **Quick obedience.** Precept Austin stresses how fast he obeyed. The Greek tense suggests he kept on rejoicing, in contrast with the rich young ruler's sadness. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-19-commentary
- **House and heart.** Matthew Henry says receiving Jesus into his house was a sign of receiving him into his heart. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-8.html
- **Not forced.** Guzik quotes Spurgeon: Christ does not push into anyone's house against their will. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-19/

**v. 7**
- **Everyone grumbled.** The Pulpit Commentary says "all" reflects the narrow spirit of the age. People couldn't imagine goodness in someone who served Rome. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/19.htm
- **What they missed.** Precept Austin says the critics assumed Jesus was approving his sin. In fact he came to convert him from it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-19-commentary

**v. 8 – a real point of disagreement**

*Is he promising something new, or describing how he already lives?*
- **Something new (the usual view).** Ellicott reads it as a new purpose. He says the idea that Zacchaeus was already a model tax collector would turn his words into a self-righteous boast, like the Pharisee's in Luke 18. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-8.htm
- Barnes agrees and says it's hard to believe anyone would make a habit of cheating people and then paying them back fourfold. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-8.htm
- **Already his practice.** William Kelly reads the words as a statement of fact about himself. Another Biblehub note says they describe a long-standing rule of life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-20.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-8.htm
- **Coffman disagrees.** He says the conversion came from receiving Jesus, not from the giving. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/luke-19.html#28-40

*What does the restitution mean?*
- **Grace first (Reformed / Puritan).** Matthew Henry says Zacchaeus isn't trying to be justified by works, as the Pharisee was. His good works show that his faith is real. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-2.htm
- Poole goes further: where you have wronged others, there can be no repentance, and so no forgiveness, without restitution as far as you're able. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-8.htm
- **Calvin** says Zacchaeus isn't offering God a share of stolen money. He pays back what he owes and also shares his lawful goods: a wolf turned into a sheep, even a shepherd. Calvin adds that this isn't a rule requiring everyone to give away half. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-8.html
- **What the Law required.** Barnes notes the Law asked for fourfold only when a thief was convicted. Someone who confessed voluntarily repaid the amount plus a fifth. Zacchaeus chose the heavier penalty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-8.htm
- **Orthodox reading.** Zacchaeus went beyond the Law. His example teaches believers to turn from their sins and atone for them, so that repentance is shown by making amends, not just by words. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/2025/02/02/1-sunday-of-zacchaeus

**v. 9**
- **Saved now.** Matthew Henry says that now he is converted, he is in effect saved from both the guilt and the power of his sins. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-1.html
- **Fruit, not merit.** Precept Austin says his giving and restitution didn't earn salvation; they were its fruit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-19-commentary
- **"Son of Abraham" (literal and spiritual).** Guzik says he was Abraham's son both by birth and by faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-19/
- The Pulpit Commentary stresses the spiritual sense: a son "in the highest and most real sense." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/19.htm
- **Orthodox reading.** The verse assures believers of God's mercy. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/2025/02/02/1-sunday-of-zacchaeus

**v. 10**
- **Who sought whom.** Guzik quotes Pate: Zacchaeus seeking Jesus (v. 3) turned out to be the result of Jesus seeking him first. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-19/
- **Ryle on grace.** Ryle (quoted in Precept Austin) says salvation is not of works but of grace. If any soul was sought and saved without deserving it, it was Zacchaeus. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-19-commentary
- **Orthodox reading.** Jesus shows God's inclusive love, beginning with people pushed to the margins. https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-steven-kostoff/a-zacchaeus-moment
- **In Orthodox worship,** this passage is always read five Sundays before Great Lent. https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-steven-kostoff/a-zacchaeus-moment
- **Orthodox tradition** also holds that Zacchaeus later travelled with Peter and became bishop of Caesarea. https://www.oca.org/saints/lives/2023/04/20/148976-apostle-zacchaeus
- **A guess, not a teaching.** Ellicott (Plumptre) floats the idea that Zacchaeus was the real-life model for the tax collector in Luke 18:10–14. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-8.htm

## Luke 19:11–24 – The Parable of the Minas

**v. 11**
- **Why Jesus told it.** Guzik says it warned that he would leave and come back before the kingdom arrived in full, and showed how to live in the meantime. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-19/
- **Calming the crowd.** MacLaren says the parable was meant to cool an expectation that could easily have flared into rebellion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-16.htm
- **Different end-times frames:**
  - GotQuestions applies the parable to the Millennial Kingdom. https://www.gotquestions.org/parable-ten-minas.html
  - Constable speaks of the kingdom being "postponed." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-16.html
  - Steven Cole describes the kingdom as present now with the King absent, and coming in full when he returns. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-88-doing-business-jesus-luke-1911-27

**v. 12**
- **What the nobleman stands for.** Adam Clarke (Methodist) says the nobleman is Jesus, and the "distant country" is his ascension. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-12.html
- **Historical background.** Many writers note that Herod's son Archelaus went to Rome to be confirmed as king, and a Jewish delegation followed to protest. Archelaus also had a palace at Jericho, where Jesus was speaking. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-88-doing-business-jesus-luke-1911-27 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/alford/luke/19.htm
- **A puzzle.** The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary notes that Archelaus was unjust and cruel, which makes the comparison a paradox, like the parables of the unjust steward and the unjust judge. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/luke-19.html

**v. 13**
- **One mina each.** Guzik says ten minas were shared out, one per servant, each worth about three months' wages. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-19/
- **What the mina means:**
  - Matthew Henry (and likewise Clarke) says it stands for the gospel, which is the same for everyone who hears it. In Matthew, the unequal talents stand for different abilities. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-13.htm
  - Cole agrees: it is the gospel shared by all believers, not just leaders. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-88-doing-business-jesus-luke-1911-27
  - Gill limits it to the gifts given to ministers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-13.htm
- **"Conduct business"** means "put this to work": the master expects growth, not just safekeeping. https://biblehub.com/luke/19-13.htm

**v. 14**
- **Who the citizens are.** Cole says first the Jewish nation ("We have no king but Caesar"), then the wider world that rejects Christ. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-88-doing-business-jesus-luke-1911-27
- Guzik stresses that the nobleman did nothing to deserve their hatred. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-19/

**v. 15**
- **The reckoning.** Biblehub's study notes take the master's return to mean the Second Coming, when he will assess how faithful his servants have been. https://biblehub.com/study/luke/19-16.htm

**vv. 16–19**
- **"Your mina."** The servants credit the master's money, not their own skill. Cole takes this to mean the power is in the gospel, not the messenger. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-19/ ; https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-88-doing-business-jesus-luke-1911-27
- **Reward in proportion.** Carson (Gospel Coalition) says each is rewarded lavishly, but in proportion to what he earned. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/devotionals/read-the-bible/2-chronicles-51-611-1-john-4-nahum-3-luke-19/

**v. 17 – disagreement over rewards**
- **Different levels of reward.** Barnes says heavenly reward will match faithfulness, but the "ten cities" aren't literal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/19-16.htm
- **Literal reign possible.** Cole allows a literal millennial reign but doesn't insist on it. He quotes Henry ("every vessel… alike full, but not alike large") and Spurgeon, who says the rewards are all of grace. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-88-doing-business-jesus-luke-1911-27
- **Reigning on earth.** Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) takes it as believers reigning with Christ over the earth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-20.html
- **More work.** Barclay says the reward for work well done is more work. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-21.html

**v. 19**
- **No praise for the second servant?** Cole notes that some see the missing "well done" as a quiet rebuke. He himself thinks the matching reward shows this servant also did well. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-88-doing-business-jesus-luke-1911-27

**vv. 20–21**
- **The cloth.** Ellicott says "kept" means he kept it all along and never tried to do more. https://biblehub.com/luke/19-20.htm
- **"Harsh man."** Gill calls the charge false and unjust, since Christ is compassionate and his yoke is easy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-21.html
- **Fear.** Constable says fear of the master was right; what was wrong was doing nothing about it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-20.html
- Wiersbe (quoting Tozer) says it is sad when Christians act from fear rather than faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-20.html

**vv. 22–23**
- **His own words judge him.** Matthew Henry says he is condemned by his crime and condemned again by his own excuse. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-20.html
- **The master isn't agreeing he is harsh.** Biblehub's notes say he just shows the servant's inconsistency. https://biblehub.com/luke/19-22.htm
- **The bank.** Cole says he should at least have deposited the money. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-88-doing-business-jesus-luke-1911-27

**v. 24 – disagreement: is the third servant saved?**
- **The question.** Cole asks directly: is he a true believer who loses his reward (1 Corinthians 3:15), or a false professor (Titus 1:16)? https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-88-doing-business-jesus-luke-1911-27
- **Not saved.** Cole sides with Bock and Ryle: the servant never knew the king. He quotes Ryle that hard thoughts of God are a mark of unconverted people. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-88-doing-business-jesus-luke-1911-27
- **A Christian who has lost out:**
  - Guzik says he stays a servant in the master's house but is left with nothing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-19/
  - The Pulpit Commentary calls him a believer who has never tasted grace, a "legal Christian." It notes that his punishment differs from the enemies' in verse 27. https://biblehub.com/luke/19-20.htm
  - Wiersbe says wasted opportunity means losing reward, and possibly losing the chance to serve. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-21.html
  - Kelly notes that the servant isn't called an enemy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/19-20.html
